CALIFORNIA CORP. CODE § 2115 — APPLICATION OF CALIFORNIA CORPORATE LAW TO OUT-OF-STATE CORPORATIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Holdings, Inc.

CALIFORNIA'S CHOICE-OF-LAW RULE FOR OUT-OF-STATE CORPORATIONS — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Holdings, Inc., a corporation originally formed under the law of Delaware, with a principal office at 100 Market Street, Suite 400, Wilmington, DE. It describes California Corporations Code Section 2115, sometimes called California's "pseudo-foreign corporation" or "quasi-California corporation" statute. That statute applies a specified list of California General Corporation Law provisions to a foreign (out-of-state) corporation, in place of the corporate law of its state of incorporation, when the corporation's average property, payroll, and sales factors and its shareholder base are predominantly connected to California, subject to statutory exemptions. This document is not this project's Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification to Transact Business in California information sheet. That document addresses the separate statutory requirement, under Chapter 21 of the General Corporation Law, that a foreign corporation obtain a certificate of qualification from the Secretary of State before transacting intrastate business in California, and the consequences of transacting business without qualifying. Section 2115 is a different statute, located in Chapter 21.5 rather than Chapter 21, and it operates independently of whether a corporation has qualified, or is even required to qualify, to transact business in California; a corporation can be subject to Section 2115's governance rules regardless of its qualification status, and qualifying to transact business does not itself trigger or avoid Section 2115. This information sheet is educational only. It does not determine whether Acme Holdings, Inc., or any other specific foreign corporation, currently meets Section 2115's statutory test, and it does not calculate any corporation's property, payroll, or sales apportionment factors or the residency of its shareholders of record.

THE TWO-PART STATUTORY TEST FOR WHETHER SECTION 2115 APPLIES TO A FOREIGN CORPORATION
California Corporations Code Section 2115 applies its governance requirements to a foreign corporation (other than a foreign association or foreign nonprofit corporation, but including a foreign parent corporation even if the parent itself does not transact intrastate business) only if two conditions are both met with respect to the corporation's latest full income year. First, the average of its property factor, payroll factor, and sales factor — the same three-factor apportionment formula used, or that would be used, on the corporation's California franchise tax return — must be more than 50 percent. Second, more than one-half of the corporation's outstanding voting securities must be held of record by persons with California addresses appearing on the corporation's books, measured as of the record date for its latest shareholders' meeting during that income year, or, if no meeting was held, as of the last day of that income year. Both conditions must be satisfied; the statute states the test in the conjunctive ("and"). For a parent corporation, the three-factor calculation is made on a consolidated, unitary basis with subsidiaries in which the parent owns more than 50 percent of the voting shares, after eliminating intercompany transactions and adjusting for minority ownership percentages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A foreign corporation (other than a foreign association or foreign nonprofit corporation but including a foreign parent corporation even though it does not itself transact intrastate business) is subject to the requirements of subdivision (b) commencing on the date specified in subdivision (d) and continuing until the date specified in subdivision (e) if: (1) The average of the property factor, the payroll factor, and the sales factor (as defined in Sections 25129, 25132, and 25134 of the Revenue and Taxation Code) with respect to it is more than 50 percent during its latest full income year and (2) more than one-half of its outstanding voting securities are held of record by persons having addresses in this state appearing on the books of the corporation on the record date for the latest meeting of shareholders held during its latest full income year or, if no meeting was held during that year, on the last day of the latest full income year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(a), California General Corporation Law, two-part test for applying Section 2115 to a foreign corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statutory test itself; it does not apply that test to any specific corporation. Determining whether a given foreign corporation meets the more-than-50-percent property/payroll/sales average requires that corporation's own apportionment data (or the data it would use if it filed a separate California return), and determining the voting-securities prong requires that corporation's specific shareholder-of-record list as of a specific record date. The statute's cross-reference to the property, payroll, and sales factor definitions in Revenue and Taxation Code Sections 25129, 25132, and 25134 is repeated here for identification only; those three Revenue and Taxation Code sections were not independently fetched or verified in this research pass, so this clause does not represent their substantive apportionment rules as separately verified primary-source text.

HOW NOMINEE-HELD SECURITIES ARE COUNTED FOR SECTION 2115'S VOTING-SECURITIES TEST
Section 2115 contains a specific rule for securities held in "nominee name" when measuring whether more than one-half of a foreign corporation's outstanding voting securities are held of record by persons with California addresses. Securities that, to the issuer's knowledge, are held in the names of broker-dealers, broker-dealer nominees (including clearing corporations), banks, or other entities holding as nominee for a beneficial owner are not counted as "outstanding" for this purpose — unless the foreign corporation requests all of its nominee holders to certify, for each beneficial owner, the number of shares held for beneficial owners with California addresses versus non-California addresses. If the corporation obtains that certification, the certified shares are then counted as outstanding and attributed to California or non-California addresses as certified, and the certification must be retained with the shareholder record and made available for inspection and copying in the same manner as the shareholder record itself. A current beneficial-owner list a nominee holder or its agent provides under federal Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 14b-1(b)(3) or 14b-2(b)(3) (as those rules stood on January 6, 1992) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is stated to be an acceptable certification for this purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the purpose of this subdivision, any securities held to the knowledge of the issuer in the names of broker-dealers, nominees for broker-dealers (including clearing corporations), or banks, associations, or other entities holding securities in a nominee name or otherwise on behalf of a beneficial owner (collectively “nominee holders”), shall not be considered outstanding. However, if the foreign corporation requests all nominee holders to certify, with respect to all beneficial owners for whom securities are held, the number of shares held for those beneficial owners having addresses (as shown on the records of the nominee holder) in this state and outside of this state, then all shares so certified shall be considered outstanding and held of record by persons having addresses either in this state or outside of this state as so certified, provided that the certification so provided shall be retained with the record of shareholders and made available for inspection and copying in the same manner as is provided in Section 1600 with respect to that record."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(a), California General Corporation Law, nominee-holder certification rule for counting voting securities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause describes a mechanical counting and certification rule, not a substantive right or obligation independent of the Section 2115(a) test described in a separate clause of this information sheet; it applies only to measuring the voting-securities prong of that test, not the separate property/payroll/sales prong. The federal Securities Exchange Act rules referenced (Rule 14b-1(b)(3) and Rule 14b-2(b)(3)) are cross-referenced by the California statute's own text as quoted here; this pass did not independently fetch or verify the text of those federal SEC rules from a federal primary source, so this clause does not represent their substantive content as separately verified.

CALIFORNIA DIRECTOR, DISTRIBUTION, AND VOTING PROVISIONS APPLIED TO A QUALIFYING FOREIGN CORPORATION
When a foreign corporation meets Section 2115(a)'s test and no exemption applies, a specified list of California General Corporation Law provisions applies to it "to the exclusion of the law of the jurisdiction in which it is incorporated." That list includes, among the director- and shareholder-governance provisions: the requirement of annual election of directors; removal of directors both without cause and by court proceeding; filling director vacancies when less than a majority of directors then in office were elected by shareholders; the directors' statutory standard of care; director liability for unlawful distributions (with two specified exclusions); indemnification of directors, officers, and others; the statutory limitations on corporate distributions in cash or property; a shareholder's liability for receiving an unlawful distribution; the requirement of an annual shareholders' meeting and the remedy if one is not timely held; shareholders' statutory right to cumulate votes in electing directors; and the supermajority-vote-requirement statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) Except as provided in subdivision (c), the following chapters and sections of this division shall apply to a foreign corporation as defined in subdivision (a) (to the exclusion of the law of the jurisdiction in which it is incorporated): Chapter 1 (general provisions and definitions), to the extent applicable to the following provisions; Section 301 (annual election of directors); Section 303 (removal of directors without cause); Section 304 (removal of directors by court proceedings); Section 305, subdivision (c) (filling of director vacancies where less than a majority in office elected by shareholders); Section 309 (directors’ standard of care); Section 316 (excluding paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) and paragraph (3) of subdivision (f)) (liability of directors for unlawful distributions); Section 317 (indemnification of directors, officers, and others); Sections 500 to 505, inclusive (limitations on corporate distributions in cash or property); Section 506 (liability of shareholder who receives unlawful distribution); Section 600, subdivisions (b) and (c) (requirement for annual shareholders’ meeting and remedy if same not timely held); Section 708, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) (shareholder’s right to cumulate votes at any election of directors); Section 710 (supermajority vote requirement);"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(b), California General Corporation Law, director/distribution/voting provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and paraphrases the list of section citations Section 2115(b) itself uses to identify which provisions apply — it does not restate the full substantive text of each cross-referenced section (for example, the specific duty-of-care standard in Section 309, or the specific indemnification rules in Section 317). Several of those underlying provisions may be the subject of other, separately verified information sheets elsewhere in this corpus addressing California corporations directly; this clause's citation is limited to the distinct fact that Section 2115(b) extends the listed provisions to a qualifying foreign corporation, not to the underlying provisions' own substantive content. This clause also does not determine whether any specific foreign corporation is currently subject to this list, which depends on the Section 2115(a) test and the effective/cessation timing described elsewhere in this information sheet.

CALIFORNIA ASSET-SALE, MERGER, REORGANIZATION, DISSENTERS'-RIGHTS, AND RECORDS PROVISIONS APPLIED TO A QUALIFYING FOREIGN CORPORATION
The remainder of Section 2115(b)'s list of provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation, in place of its home jurisdiction's law, covers: the statutory limitation on sale of assets; the statutory limitation on mergers; the first sentence of the statute governing limitations on conversions, together with the separate statute setting the requirements of conversions; the entire chapter of the General Corporation Law governing reorganizations; the entire chapter governing dissenters' (appraisal) rights; the statutes on corporate records and reports; the statute authorizing action by the Attorney General; and the entire chapter governing shareholders' rights of inspection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Section 1001, subdivision (d) (limitations on sale of assets); Section 1101, subdivision (b) (limitations on mergers); Section 1151 (first sentence only) (limitations on conversions); Section 1152 (requirements of conversions); Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 1200) (reorganizations); Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 1300) (dissenters’ rights); Sections 1500 and 1501 (records and reports); Section 1508 (action by Attorney General); Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 1600) (rights of inspection)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(b), California General Corporation Law, asset-sale/merger/reorganization/dissenters'-rights/records provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: As with the director/distribution/voting list, this clause quotes Section 2115(b)'s own enumeration of cross-referenced provisions; it does not restate the substantive content of those provisions (for example, the specific inspection procedures in the rights-of-inspection chapter, or the specific appraisal procedure in the dissenters'-rights chapter), several of which may be addressed by other, separately verified information sheets elsewhere in this corpus for California corporations directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific foreign corporation is currently subject to this list.

STATUTORY EXEMPTIONS FROM SECTION 2115
Section 2115 does not apply to a foreign corporation that falls within either of two exemptions, even if the corporation would otherwise meet the property/payroll/sales and voting-securities test. The first exemption covers a corporation with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market. The second exemption covers a corporation all of whose voting shares (other than directors' qualifying shares) are owned, directly or indirectly, by a corporation or corporations that are not themselves subject to Section 2115.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) This section does not apply to any corporation (1) with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market, or (2) if all of its voting shares (other than directors’ qualifying shares) are owned directly or indirectly by a corporation or corporations not subject to this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(c), California General Corporation Law, exchange-listing and wholly-owned-subsidiary exemptions from Section 2115 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: The specific exchange names in the first exemption (NYSE American, NASDAQ Global Market, NASDAQ Capital Market) reflect the version of Section 2115 as amended by Statutes 2022, Chapter 617 (SB 1202), effective January 1, 2023, which updated older exchange terminology (for example, the statute no longer refers to the American Stock Exchange by that name). This clause reflects the statute's current text as fetched on the date shown; it does not independently verify which securities exchanges any specific corporation's securities are actually listed on, and does not address whether a corporation exempt under the second prong might itself later become subject to Section 2115 if its parent corporation's own exempt status changes.

WHEN SECTION 2115(B)'S REQUIREMENTS BEGIN TO APPLY
Section 2115 does not apply its list of California provisions the moment a foreign corporation's property/payroll/sales and voting-securities figures cross the statutory threshold. Instead, the requirements of subdivision (b) become applicable only as of the first day of the corporation's first income year that either (1) commences on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the Section 2115(a) tests were met, or (2) commences on or after entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall become applicable to a foreign corporation only upon the first day of the first income year of the corporation (1) commencing on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the tests referred to in subdivision (a) have been met or (2) commencing on or after the entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(d), California General Corporation Law, effective-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements begin to apply (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) becomes applicable; it does not calculate the specific effective date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires knowing that corporation's income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first met the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address what happens if a corporation's income year changes during the relevant period, a scenario the statute's text does not itself resolve.

WHEN SECTION 2115(B)'S REQUIREMENTS CEASE TO APPLY
Just as Section 2115(b)'s requirements do not begin immediately upon meeting the statutory test, they do not end immediately upon ceasing to meet it. The requirements cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation either (1) at the end of the first income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the Section 2115(a) tests was not met, or (2) at the end of the income year during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met — provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of that income year.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(e) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation (1) at the end of the first income year of the corporation immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the tests referred to in subdivision (a) is not met or (2) at the end of the income year of the corporation during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met, provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of the income year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(e), California General Corporation Law, cessation-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements stop applying (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) ceases to apply; it does not calculate the specific cessation date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires that corporation's own income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first failed to meet the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address the effect of a court order that is later reversed on appeal after the relevant income year has already closed.

DUTY TO DISCLOSE SECTION 2115(B) STATUS ON WRITTEN REQUEST
A foreign corporation that is subject to Section 2115(b)'s requirements must advise, in writing and within 30 days of receiving a written request, any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of the indemnification statute, Section 317), and any creditor of the corporation, whether or not the corporation is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. If a party obtains a final determination from a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation either failed to provide this information or provided incorrect information of the kind required, the court has discretion to include in its judgment recovery, from the corporation, of all court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees the party incurred in the legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(f) Any foreign corporation that is subject to the requirements of subdivision (b) shall advise any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of Section 317) and any creditor of the corporation in writing, within 30 days of receipt of written request for that information, whether or not it is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. Any party who obtains a final determination by a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation failed to provide to the party information required to be provided by this subdivision or provided the party information of the kind required to be provided by this subdivision that was incorrect, then the court, in its discretion, shall have the power to include in its judgment recovery by the party from the corporation of all court costs and reasonable attorneys’ fees incurred in that legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(f), California General Corporation Law, duty to disclose Section 2115(b) status on written request and cost/fee-shifting remedy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2115.)
  Known gap: This clause describes a disclosure obligation and an associated cost-and-fee-shifting judicial remedy triggered by a specific procedural sequence (a written request, a 30-day response window, and a final court determination); it does not itself create a general private right of action for damages beyond that cost-and-fee recovery, and the statute's text does not define what would make attorneys' fees "reasonable" in a given case. This clause also does not address whether, or how, a corporation must respond to an oral request, or a request from someone outside the specific categories the statute lists (shareholder of record, officer, director, employee, Section 317 agent, or creditor).

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — PSEUDO-FOREIGN CORPORATION (SECTION 2115) INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme Holdings, Inc.'s potential status under California Corporations Code Section 2115 was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes.

Executed on April 1, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________

It is not a determination that Acme Holdings, Inc. or any other entity is or is not currently subject to Section 2115(b), does not calculate any corporation's property, payroll, sales, or voting-securities figures, and does not constitute legal advice. It also does not address the separate statutory requirement that a foreign corporation obtain a certificate of qualification before transacting intrastate business in California, which this project addresses in a separate information sheet.]

This clause does not determine whether any specific foreign corporation is currently subject to this list.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2115 does not apply to a foreign corporation that falls within either of two exemptions, even if the corporation would otherwise meet the property/payroll/sales and voting-securities test. The first exemption covers a corporation with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market. The second exemption covers a corporation all of whose voting shares (other than directors' qualifying shares) are owned, directly or indirectly, by a corporation or corporations that are not themselves subject to Section 2115.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, exchange-listing and wholly-owned-subsidiary exemptions from Section 2115
citations.quote: (c) This section does not apply to any corporation (1) with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market, or (2) if all of its voting shares (other than directors’ qualifying shares) are owned directly or indirectly by a corporation or corporations not subject to this section.

expectedJSON.gap: The specific exchange names in the first exemption (NYSE American, NASDAQ Global Market, NASDAQ Capital Market) reflect the version of Section 2115 as amended by Statutes 2022, Chapter 617 (SB 1202), effective January 1, 2023, which updated older exchange terminology (for example, the statute no longer refers to the American Stock Exchange by that name). This clause reflects the statute's current text as fetched on the date shown; it does not independently verify which securities exchanges any specific corporation's securities are actually listed on, and does not address whether a corporation exempt under the second prong might itself later become subject to Section 2115 if its parent corporation's own exempt status changes.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2115 does not apply its list of California provisions the moment a foreign corporation's property/payroll/sales and voting-securities figures cross the statutory threshold. Instead, the requirements of subdivision (b) become applicable only as of the first day of the corporation's first income year that either (1) commences on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the Section 2115(a) tests were met, or (2) commences on or after entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, effective-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements begin to apply
citations.quote: (d) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall become applicable to a foreign corporation only upon the first day of the first income year of the corporation (1) commencing on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the tests referred to in subdivision (a) have been met or (2) commencing on or after the entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) becomes applicable; it does not calculate the specific effective date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires knowing that corporation's income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first met the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address what happens if a corporation's income year changes during the relevant period, a scenario the statute's text does not itself resolve.

expectedJSON.body: Just as Section 2115(b)'s requirements do not begin immediately upon meeting the statutory test, they do not end immediately upon ceasing to meet it. The requirements cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation either (1) at the end of the first income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the Section 2115(a) tests was not met, or (2) at the end of the income year during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met — provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of that income year.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, cessation-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements stop applying
citations.quote: (e) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation (1) at the end of the first income year of the corporation immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the tests referred to in subdivision (a) is not met or (2) at the end of the income year of the corporation during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met, provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of the income year.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) ceases to apply; it does not calculate the specific cessation date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires that corporation's own income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first failed to meet the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address the effect of a court order that is later reversed on appeal after the relevant income year has already closed.

expectedJSON.body: A foreign corporation that is subject to Section 2115(b)'s requirements must advise, in writing and within 30 days of receiving a written request, any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of the indemnification statute, Section 317), and any creditor of the corporation, whether or not the corporation is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. If a party obtains a final determination from a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation either failed to provide this information or provided incorrect information of the kind required, the court has discretion to include in its judgment recovery, from the corporation, of all court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees the party incurred in the legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, duty to disclose Section 2115(b) status on written request and cost/fee-shifting remedy
citations.quote: (f) Any foreign corporation that is subject to the requirements of subdivision (b) shall advise any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of Section 317) and any creditor of the corporation in writing, within 30 days of receipt of written request for that information, whether or not it is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. Any party who obtains a final determination by a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation failed to provide to the party information required to be provided by this subdivision or provided the party information of the kind required to be provided by this subdivision that was incorrect, then the court, in its discretion, shall have the power to include in its judgment recovery by the party from the corporation of all court costs and reasonable attorneys’ fees incurred in that legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause describes a disclosure obligation and an associated cost-and-fee-shifting judicial remedy triggered by a specific procedural sequence (a written request, a 30-day response window, and a final court determination); it does not itself create a general private right of action for damages beyond that cost-and-fee recovery, and the statute's text does not define what would make attorneys' fees "reasonable" in a given case. This clause also does not address whether, or how, a corporation must respond to an oral request, or a request from someone outside the specific categories the statute lists (shareholder of record, officer, director, employee, Section 317 agent, or creditor).
